info.title: Jarvis Gateway
info.description: Contract for the Jarvis Android app. Base URL: https://gw03.tail9662e3.ts.net/api

get.description:
`status` repeats: `?status=active&status=awaiting`. Single-valued was a
filter row that could only ever answer one chip (joy A6, 2026-08-20).

All three are typed rather than checked by hand, so the enum and the date
format appear in `openapi.json` and FastAPI rejects bad input before it
reaches a query. Untyped, they were handed straight to Postgres: an unknown
status hit an enum cast and 500'd, and the dates 500'd on *valid* input too,
because `due_date` is a date column and asyncpg will not coerce a string.

Opening a task's session needs exactly this one task — whether it is
terminal decides whether the composer appears. Without it the app pages
`GET /tasks` until it finds the id (joy A4, 2026-08-20).

Returns the task bare: a GET returns the resource, a mutation wraps it.

patch.description:
Direct UI manipulation of cheap reversible fields — no proposal.
AI-initiated mutations confirm; a menu tap cannot misparse.

Routed through `update_task` rather than a per-field setter so that a body
carrying several keys is one statement and one row version. The app sends
them singly today, but two setters would make "both" mean two writes and a
window between them.

`accepted_failure` is here for that reason and one more (item 108): a flag
with no write path can only be set in psql, which means it is never set, and
the dashboard keeps leading with a failure Joy decided months ago to live
with. Accepting with a reason is ONE call — `{"accepted_failure": true,
"accepted_reason": "..."}` — precisely so the flag and the sentence cannot
end up in different row versions.

post.description:
Confirmed from either path, because cancelling is not cheaply reversible.

`scope` distinguishes skipping one firing from stopping the rule.

get.description: The device alarm mirror. Replace-the-window on the client, not merge.

What happened. The counterpart to /occurrences/upcoming (v2 plan §3).

Every field here has been stored since 0001 and none of it was readable:
`upcoming` is the only occurrence read on the API and it looks forward only.
So this ships with no migration and no backfill — the history is already
complete for every firing this system has resolved.

`bucket` chooses which day the range filters on and is echoed back on the
response. `resolved` is the day it was ANSWERED, `due` is the day it was
DUE; they diverge on anything resolved late, which is most of what a
dashboard about slipping wants to look at. Both dates are on every row
regardless, so the client never derives one from the other (§3.2).

NOTE FOR ANYONE COMPUTING LATENESS FROM THESE ROWS: `scheduled_for` is the
deadline as it stood when the firing resolved, not as it was set. An
extension overwrites it in place, so a firing extended twice reports the
extended deadline and looks punctual. Board item 69 is the fix; until the
event stream exists, treat `extensions_used > 0` as "this row understates
how late it was".

v2 plan §6, v1: over tasks alone.

"The app renders; the gateway computes every number. No streaks,
percentages or day-bucketing on the client" — so this returns finished
arithmetic. The window is in LOCAL DAYS and filters on `scheduled_date`, a
stored column, because §3.2 forbids deriving a calendar day from a
timestamp anywhere.

Two of §6's four words are answerable over tasks. `missed` needs routines
and `stale` needs to-dos; both are ABSENT rather than zero, because a zero
reads as "nothing missed" and that would be a claim this cannot support.

READ `provenance` BEFORE PRESENTING ANY OF THIS AS MEASUREMENT. The event
stream landed on 2026-09-01 and everything before it is one reconstructed
row per firing with no extension history, so `drifting` can only speak for
firings whose whole life was observed. `firings_without_history` counts what
that leaves out, so a short drift list cannot be mistaken for a clean one.

Defaults to the last seven local days INCLUDING today, which is the window
the word "lately" means.

Read ONE firing, in whatever state it is in (board items 83, 88).

Declared after `/occurrences/upcoming` and `/occurrences/history` on
purpose: FastAPI matches in declaration order, and this path would
otherwise swallow both and 422 on the path-int conversion.

Until now every occurrence read on the API went through a window —
`upcoming` looking forward, `history` looking back — so there was no way to
ask about one occurrence by id at all. `AlarmReceiver` builds its
notification at fire time from the mirror, and needs a way to check whether
the deadline it is about to announce has moved.

THIS IS A COMPLEMENT TO THE MIRROR, NOT A REPLACEMENT FOR IT. Fire time is
exactly when the phone is most likely to be off the tailnet, so the client
must still fall back to its own row when this call fails — which is why the
mirror had to be fixed first (`upcoming_occurrences`), and why this route
alone would have patched the button and left the mirror wrong.

No window, no status filter: a resolved firing answers here too, and its
`resolved_at` is the honest answer to "has this already been dealt with".

post.description:
One second chance on a missed deadline (joy 07 §3.2).

Not a proposal. The four buttons on an overdue nudge are direct UI
manipulation of a cheap, reversible thing — the same reasoning that lets
PATCH /tasks set a priority flag without a confirmation card. Routing this
through the model would also make answering a nudge cost an LLM call and
could misparse a tap, which is exactly what a button is for.

Occurrence-scoped, so extending Monday's firing leaves the weekly rule
alone.

Mark this firing done (joy 07 §3.2).

The gateway had NO completion endpoint at all until this one: `propose_complete`
existed as a tool and `/tasks/{id}/cancel` as a route, but nothing completed
a task outside the confirm flow. Needed regardless of the follow-up loop.

Task-scoped completion is deliberately still absent. Finishing one firing of
a weekly rule must not close the series, and an endpoint that could do
either depending on a flag is how that mistake gets made.

get.description:
Browsable conversation history (joy addendum §2).

General chat is a series of conversations, not one thread — you ask about
something, get pointed at a task, and that exchange is worth looking back
at. Reopening needs nothing new: `GET /sessions/{id}/messages` already
returns persisted `components`, so a past disambiguation renders with its
option buttons intact.

post.description:
Get-or-create for a task binding: a task has exactly one session and
reopening it is the normal path, so this no longer 409s on the second call.
See `agentrepo.create_session`.

get.description:
"Show more" on a disambiguation list (joy A3, 2026-08-20).

A pure read: it appends nothing to the transcript and calls no model. The
alternative was redeeming the cursor through `POST /messages`, which would
appear as something the user said and spend a model call to page a list the
server already has.

The cursor carries the search, so this holds no state between calls.

The routine version to render, whole.

THE APP CACHES THIS AND WORKS FROM IT OFFLINE. The routine tab has to render
off the tailnet (§4.2), so this is a fetch-once-and-keep object, not a
per-view read. Everything needed to resolve a logical day locally is on it:
every weekday's declared boundaries, every slot in `position` order.

`on` picks the version effective on that local day — the latest
`effective_from` not after it — because an edit takes effect from tomorrow
and days already measured keep the plan they were measured against (§4.6).
`version_id` reads one directly, which is what a client showing an old
week's log needs.

What logical day it is, and what is running. A CROSS-CHECK.

NOT LOAD-BEARING, and that is a decision rather than an omission (§4.2,
tracker item 84). The app resolves the logical day locally from boundaries
this server declared, and must keep doing so — a routine tab that needed a
round trip to know what day it is would be blank exactly when someone is
checking whether they did the gym. This route exists so the two answers can
be compared, and as the answer before a version has been fetched. If they
ever disagree that is a bug worth finding, and it is only findable because
both exist.

The start log over a range of LOGICAL days.

Both dates are required: a default window here would have to pick between
"this routine week" and "the last seven days", and those differ by which
weekday the week starts on — a question the client answers and this route
should not guess at.

post.description:
One tap: I am starting this. There is no stop (§4.4).

Starting the next slot is what ends this one, so a slot's real duration is
the gap to the following start — which means doing gym after uni records
itself without anyone declaring an order was broken, and that variation is
the whole reason the feature exists.

Idempotent per (version, slot, logical day): a second tap corrects the
first in place. The correction is not lost — the projection moves and the
event stream keeps both taps (§4.6).

delete.description:
Undo a start. A mis-tap should not need a whole editing surface.

Answers `ok` whether or not there was one to clear — clearing an already
clear slot is the state the caller asked for. A `cleared` event is appended
only when something actually was.

get.description:
The list. The BACKLOG is `undated_only=true`, not a second route.

§5.2 gives undated to-dos "their own place in the UI — a backlog". That is a
filter over one ordering, not a different collection: a to-do gains and
loses a deadline over its life and must not appear to move between two
lists when it does.

Ordered by deadline with NULLS LAST, then by how recently it moved.

SUB-TASKS ARE EXCLUDED BY DEFAULT (item 135) — `include_children=true` to
have them as peers, `parent_id=` to fetch one parent's children. Otherwise
the list doubles in length the day the feature is used and every child shows
twice: once inside its parent's `child_count` and again on a row of its own.

That default was free to pick exactly once, because it ships in the same
deploy that makes a child possible: today it returns precisely what it
returned before, for every row that exists.

`priority` is repeatable and matches the `status` convention rather than
inventing a second one for the same shape of filter.

post.description:
Direct creation, no proposal.

A task is proposed-and-confirmed because the model parses "next Thursday"
and can misread it. A to-do typed into a form cannot be misparsed — the same
reasoning that lets `PATCH /tasks` set a flag directly. When the agent gets
a tool for this it will go through propose-and-confirm like everything else
it does.

patch.description:
Only what is sent is changed.

`due_at: null` PRESENT clears the deadline; omitting it leaves it alone.
Those are different requests and `exclude_unset` is what keeps them
different — clearing a deadline is an ordinary edit here (§5.2), not an
error to be defended against.

get.description:
What has happened to this to-do, newest first (§5, tracker item 136).

WHY IT IS WORTH A ROUTE. The dashboard can say a to-do has gone stale; only
this can say whether it was touched-and-deferred or genuinely forgotten, and
those two are indistinguishable in `updated_at` — which is the field a
reader would otherwise reach for and be misled by.

404 ON AN UNKNOWN TO-DO rather than an empty list. Every to-do has at least
a `created` event, so `events: []` is never the honest answer for one that
exists, and answering it for a wrong id would hide the caller's bug. Same
rule as everywhere else here: absence and emptiness are different, and the
response must not merge them.

The table is append-only — never updated, never deleted — so a page of this
is a page of what actually happened rather than of what is currently
believed.

post.description:
Attach an existing reminder to this to-do (§5.1).

A task, not a copy. Setting a reminder on a to-do means creating the task
through the flow that already fires, chases and extends, then pointing at
it — which is what keeps one deadline chased by one system rather than two.

Idempotent: linking a task already linked here changes nothing and answers
the same to-do.

delete.description:
Detach a reminder. THE TASK SURVIVES — it keeps firing, and its own
routes still resolve it. Unlinking says "this reminder is not about that
to-do", which is not the same as "stop reminding me".

get.description:
Stored summaries, newest first.

§7 wants these STORED rather than generated on view, so this is a plain
read: "what did I get done last Tuesday" is answered by a record written at
the time, not by re-deriving it now from data that has moved since.

Omitting `tag` returns every summary including the per-group ones. Passing
it narrows to that group; there is no way to ask for "overall only" because
`tag` is null on exactly one row per period and the client can see that.

post.description:
Write one now.

Exists so a summary can be produced and READ before the scheduler is
allowed to write one every day — `SUMMARIES_AUTO` defaults off precisely so
that judgement is made on real output rather than on the design.

`facts_only` skips the model call, which is the cheapest way to see exactly
what the model would be given.

AgentResponse.title: AgentResponse
AgentResponse.description: Structured, never bare text — the app renders cards and buttons.

CreateTodoBody.title: CreateTodoBody
CreateTodoBody.description:
Direct creation, no proposal.

A task is proposed-and-confirmed because the model parses "next Thursday"
and can misread it. A to-do typed into a form cannot be misparsed — the
same reasoning that lets `PATCH /tasks` set a priority flag directly (§5.4
of the parent plan). The agent will get a tool for this later; it will go
through propose-and-confirm like everything else it does.

Dashboard.title: Dashboard
Dashboard.description:
v2 plan §6, v1: over tasks alone.

ALL FOUR of §6's words are answerable now: `failed` and `drifting` over
tasks, `missed` and routine `drifting` over slots, `stale` over undated
to-dos. Each arrived with its domain rather than as a zero standing in for
one — which is the rule that kept `missed` out until routines existed and
`stale` out until to-dos did.

DashboardPeriod.title: DashboardPeriod
DashboardPeriod.description:
The window, and which day it was bucketed on.

`bucketed_by` is `due` and is stated rather than assumed: §3 settled that
"what did I miss" is the day something was DUE and "what did I get done" is
the day it was ANSWERED. This screen is the first question, so it filters on
`scheduled_date` — a stored local day, never derived from a timestamp.

DashboardPolicy.title: DashboardPolicy
DashboardPolicy.description:
The thresholds, on the wire, because a number the client cannot see is a
number nobody can argue with.

`drift_threshold_minutes` is DERIVED, not invented: grace plus everything
the extension allowance buys is the longest the system was ever willing to
wait before giving up. A completion later than that is later than the
gateway's own tolerance, which is a standard already agreed rather than a
line drawn for this screen. §4.2 rejected a threshold "nobody can justify";
this one is justified by policy that already exists.

`drift_min_firings` is 3 — the smallest number for which "consistently"
means anything. Two late completions are an anecdote.

DRIFT IS PER-DOMAIN AND SO IS ITS DERIVATION (joy, item 93). 135 minutes is
a TASK threshold: it would never fire on a 90-minute gym slot at all, and a
gym slot started half an hour late is drift. The routine threshold is
derived from `grace_minutes` alone — this system's declared unit of "a delay
that does not count" — and lands on the 15 minutes the app currently
hardcodes, with a reason instead of a guess.

DashboardProvenance.title: DashboardProvenance
DashboardProvenance.description:
How much of this screen is observation and how much is reconstruction.

NOT OPTIONAL AND NOT A FOOTNOTE. The event stream landed on 2026-09-01;
everything before it is one backfilled row per firing with no extension
history at all. A dashboard that presented reconstructed history as
measurement would be exactly the failure `backfilled` was added to prevent,
so the response carries its own provenance and the client cannot fail to
have been told.

DashboardTotals.title: DashboardTotals
DashboardTotals.description:
Counts of FIRINGS, not of tasks. A daily reminder that lapsed six days
running is six failures and one task, and the headline means the first.

DriftingSlot.title: DriftingSlot
DriftingSlot.description:
§6 `drifting` for routines: started consistently, but not near plan.

ABSOLUTE DEVIATION, so starting early counts too — matching the app's
`SlotRow.drifted`, which is `|actual - planned| > tolerance`. The two sides
have to mean the same thing by the word or the screen and the dashboard
will disagree about the same slot.

DriftingTask.title: DriftingTask
DriftingTask.description:
§6 `drifting`: completed consistently, but not near the plan.

COMPLETED FIRINGS ONLY. A firing that lapsed is `failed`, and counting it
here would fold the two words together — its slip is the system's whole
tolerance by construction, so it would dominate the median and say nothing.

MEASURED AGAINST THE ORIGINAL DEADLINE, which is why this needed the event
stream: `extend_occurrence` overwrites `scheduled_for`, so the projection
compares a completion against a deadline that was already moved to meet it.

ExtendOccurrenceBody.title: ExtendOccurrenceBody
ExtendOccurrenceBody.description:
A second chance, in minutes (07 §3.2).

Typed as a literal so the choices appear in openapi.json and FastAPI rejects
anything else with a 422 before it reaches a query — the same reasoning as
the `status` filter on GET /tasks. Kept in step with config.EXTENSION_MINUTES,
which is what the app renders as buttons; a Literal cannot be built from a
runtime value without losing the generated schema, so the two are asserted
equal at import instead of one deriving from the other.

FailingTask.title: FailingTask
FailingTask.description:
§6 `failed`, grouped by task so the repeat offenders are visible.

Every number here survives in the projection — `status` is stored per firing
and nothing overwrites it — so this half of the dashboard is honest over the
whole history, unlike `drifting`.

GenerateSummaryBody.title: GenerateSummaryBody
GenerateSummaryBody.description:
A deliberate act, which is why it is a POST with a body rather than a
side effect of reading.

HistoryOccurrence.title: HistoryOccurrence
HistoryOccurrence.description:
One resolved firing, for the dashboard (v2 plan §3).

Carries BOTH days on purpose, because they answer different questions and
the plan has not yet chosen between them:

  `scheduled_date` — the local day it was DUE. "What did I miss."
  `resolved_at`    — the instant it was answered. "What did I get done."

Completing yesterday's reminder this morning is due=yesterday,
answered=today, and neither is the wrong answer. Both are stored already, so
the client never has to pick one by deriving the other.

MissedSlot.title: MissedSlot
MissedSlot.description:
§6 `missed`: a tracked routine slot never started.

NOT THE SAME AS FAILED, and §4.4 says why in its own words: this "cannot
distinguish 'I skipped gym' from 'I did gym and forgot to tap'". So it is a
count of unrecorded slots, not of failures, and the day-end prompt §4.4
wants is what would make it stronger.

NewTaskComponent.title: NewTaskComponent
NewTaskComponent.description:
A way out of a general session that was asked to create something.

A general session has no create tool and correctly declines — but that
leaves the user having already said what they wanted, with nowhere to go.
The app renders this as a button that opens a NEW unbound session and sends
`seed` immediately, so nothing is retyped (joy addendum §4).

The invariant is untouched: this session still creates nothing, and the new
session binds only on confirmation. Seeding skips the typing, not the
confirmation.

Occurrence.title: Occurrence
Occurrence.description:
One firing of a task (joy 07 §3.1).

Occurrence-scoped, not task-scoped, and this is the whole reason the table
exists (parent §2.5): finishing Monday's gym session must not close the
weekly rule.

OccurrenceEnvelope.title: OccurrenceEnvelope
OccurrenceEnvelope.description:
What /extend and /complete answer with (07 §3.2).

Both, not one: extending changes the firing AND (for a one-shot) the task's
own due time, and completing resolves the firing while possibly leaving a
recurring parent untouched. The app needs to see which of those happened.

OverdueComponent.title: OverdueComponent
OverdueComponent.description:
The agent asking whether a missed thing got done (joy 07 §3.3).

This is the first component the SERVER originates. Every other one answers a
user turn; this one is posted into the task's session by the scheduler when
a deadline passes, which is what makes the agent able to initiate at all.

It is a MESSAGE, not only a push notification, because one session per task
is the architecture (parent §2.2) and scrolling back has to show the agent
asking and what was answered — exactly as a resolved confirm card does
(§5.3). A nudge living only in a notification vanishes with the notification
and leaves no record that you were asked.

`extensions_used == extensions_allowed` is the app's signal that no second
chance remains, so this renders with "Mark done" alone and no extend
buttons. That case is also the FINAL message: the firing has already been
recorded `incomplete` by the time it is sent (§3.4). Deliberately derived
rather than carried as a separate flag — the doc fixes this shape, and a
field the app has not been built to read is worth less than one it can
compute.

`grace_minutes` and `extension_minutes` are policy the app needs and must
not hardcode (09 §2.4, §5). The grace value is load-bearing rather than
informational: under 09 §2 the loop runs on timeouts, so the app schedules a
catch-up poll for `grace_minutes + small` after a nudge, to learn about a
transition it did not initiate (09 §7). An app assuming 15 goes out of sync
the moment this is tuned here, which is the whole reason it is tunable.

Both are sent before the app reads them: §4.5 has it tolerating unknown
fields, so they are inert until consumed and correct the day they are.

PatchTaskBody.title: PatchTaskBody
PatchTaskBody.description:
Direct UI manipulation of cheap, reversible fields — never a proposal
(plan §5.4). A tap cannot misparse, and tapping again undoes it exactly.

EVERY KEY IS OPTIONAL AND THE APP SENDS ONE AT A TIME: `is_priority` alone
for a star tap, `description` alone for a checklist tick. Requiring all of
them would make a star tap resend a description it did not touch, which is a
lost-update race against a tick landing in the same second.

`accepted_failure` belongs HERE and not behind a proposal, by §5.4's own
rule: it is a cheap, reversible field set by a direct tap. A tap cannot
misparse, and tapping again undoes it exactly. Without a write path the flag
could only be set in psql, which means it would never be set at all — the
PATCH is the part that makes item 108 real rather than theoretical.

THE THREE STATES OF A KEY ARE DELIBERATELY DIFFERENT:

  absent  -> leave the column alone. The app's serialiser omits unset
             fields (`explicitNulls=false`), so this is what a one-key
             patch produces and it must be the safe case.
  ""      -> clear the description. Explicit, and the only way to empty it.
  null    -> 422. Never sent by the app, and the alternative is worse than
             an error: `update_task` skips nulls, so a null would return
             200 with nothing changed. A tick that silently does nothing is
             exactly the failure joy asked to avoid — better a visible error
             the app can surface than a checkbox that quietly reverts.

An empty body is 422 for the same reason: it can only be a bug on the
caller's side, and answering 200 would hide it.

`accepted_reason` follows the same three states, with `""` meaning "clear
the sentence but stay accepted" — the reason is stored as NULL, because a
reason that is the empty string is not a reason. `accepted_at` is NOT
accepted here: when something was decided is the server's to record, and a
client that could set it could backdate a decision.

PatchTodoBody.title: PatchTodoBody
PatchTodoBody.description:
Every field optional; only what is sent is changed.

`exclude_unset` distinguishes "not mentioned" from "set to null", which
matters here more than anywhere else in this API: clearing a deadline is a
real, ordinary edit (§5.2), so `due_at: null` has to mean something
different from omitting it.

ProposalSummary.title: ProposalSummary
ProposalSummary.description:
What the confirmation card renders. `recurrence_text` is load-bearing:
the eval measured malformed recurrence arguments at ~1 in 5 on the
Nth-weekday pattern, and a human reading this before confirming is the
only thing that catches a wrong day set.

GUARANTEE: `due_date` IS ALWAYS PRESENT WHEN `due_at` IS (joy, board item
63). Both stay optional because a `cancel` or `complete` proposal carries
neither, and a conditional invariant is not expressible in JSON Schema —
so it is enforced below instead of typed.

The client must never derive the calendar day from `due_at` itself. That is
§3.2's rule and the reason `due_date` exists at all: the phone deriving it
applies the PHONE's timezone, which is right only while the phone and the
server are in the same one. A proposal is the worst place to get it wrong,
because confirming the card is what writes the task and the only check on
a wrong day is a human reading it.

RecordStartBody.title: RecordStartBody
RecordStartBody.description:
`version_id` IS REQUIRED AND IS NOT INFERRED FROM `on`.

The app resolved the logical day against a version it had already fetched,
so it is the only party that knows which one. Inferring it here would
re-bucket a start whenever a version changed between the fetch and the tap
— the exact failure §4.4 put the version first to prevent.

Routine.title: Routine
Routine.description:
A routine version, whole. The app caches this and resolves logical days
against it offline (§4.2) — the routine tab must render off the tailnet.

RoutineCategory.title: RoutineCategory
RoutineCategory.description:
Identity and classification, merged for the wire.

They are stored apart — `key`/`label` on the routine, `cls` on the version
— because a cross-version rollup joins on identity and reclassifying a
category must not restate last month (§4.5, item 84). The client has no use
for that split: it renders one list.

RoutineDay.title: RoutineDay
RoutineDay.description:
One weekday's plan, with its boundaries DECLARED.

All seven cross midnight (§4.2). There is no default and no branch: a
client that treats a missing boundary as midnight would silently delete
Monday's 23:00–01:00 slot.

RoutineNow.title: RoutineNow
RoutineNow.description:
The gateway's own answer to "what logical day is it, and what is running".

A CROSS-CHECK AND A PRE-FETCH ANSWER, NOT THE SOURCE OF TRUTH (§4.2, item
84b). The app computes this locally from boundaries this server declared,
because the routine tab has to render off the tailnet — a tab that needed a
round trip to know what day it is would be blank exactly when someone is
checking whether they did the gym. This route exists so the two can be
compared: if they ever disagree, that is a bug worth finding, and it is only
findable because both exist.

RoutineProvenance.title: RoutineProvenance
RoutineProvenance.description:
Whether the routine numbers are measuring anything yet.

THE SAME TRAP AS `drifting` ON THE TASK SIDE, in a new place. Before anyone
has tapped a slot, every tracked slot in every finished day is "never
started" — so a naive `missed` would report the whole week as missed and be
indistinguishable from "the routine tab has not been used". §4.4 admits the
ambiguity; this makes it visible instead of letting it read as failure.

So `missed` counts only within days that carry at least one start. A day
with none says nothing about what was missed, and counting it would put the
loudest possible number in front of someone who has simply not started
logging.

RoutineSlot.title: RoutineSlot
RoutineSlot.description:
One contiguous block. `ends_at <= starts_at` means it crosses midnight,
which is ordinary here — Friday's shift runs 13:45 to 00:15.

SectionsResponse.title: SectionsResponse
SectionsResponse.description: One round trip for the whole Tasks tab first paint (§2.7).

SessionSummary.title: SessionSummary
SessionSummary.description:
One line per conversation for the Chat history list (joy addendum §2).

A task session is one thread bound to a task forever; general chat is a
series of conversations, and the ones where you asked about something and
got pointed at a task are worth keeping. Computed here rather than by the
app fetching every session's first page just to label a list.

SlotStart.title: SlotStart
SlotStart.description: When a tracked slot was actually begun. There is no stop (§4.4).

StaleTodo.title: StaleTodo
StaleTodo.description: §6 `stale`: an undated to-do untouched past a threshold. Cannot fail.

Summary.title: Summary
Summary.description:
One stored summary. §7.

TWO THINGS, AND ONLY ONE OF THEM IS GENERATED. `facts` is counted by the
gateway and is as trustworthy as the dashboard; `text` is written by a model
FROM those facts and is an interpretation of them. Both are on the wire so a
reader can hold the sentence against the arithmetic it came from — and so a
client can render the numbers even when the prose is missing.

SummaryCount.title: SummaryCount
SummaryCount.description:
How many, and which ones. Names as well as a count because §7's summaries
are about what you did, and "3 reminders completed" is a worse sentence than
the three titles.

SummaryFacts.title: SummaryFacts
SummaryFacts.description:
The counted half of a summary, TYPED.

It was an untyped object for about an hour after shipping, which left the
client guessing at the shape of the only trustworthy half of the response.
Typed here so it appears in `openapi.json` and the app has a contract rather
than a convention — the numbers are the part §6 says the gateway owns, and
handing them over as an unspecified map would give that ownership back by
the back door.

Grows by OPTIONAL fields as domains are added, which is additive and does
not break a client that has not heard of them.

SummaryReminderVerb.title: SummaryReminderVerb
SummaryReminderVerb.description: The reminder verbs a summary counts — a strict subset of `ReminderVerb`, and the only keys `SummaryFacts.reminders` can carry. §7 summarises what YOU did, so the machinery verbs are left out: `asked`, `extended` and `revived` are the loop chasing you rather than an outcome. READ `cancelled` NARROWLY — it is the `cancelled` event alone, meaning a firing somebody decided against. A reminder whose deadline MOVED is `superseded`, a different word, and it is not counted here at all, so this number is decisions and never reschedules.

SummaryTodoVerb.title: SummaryTodoVerb
SummaryTodoVerb.description: The to-do verbs a summary counts — a strict subset of `TodoVerb`, and the only keys `SummaryFacts.todos` can carry. The edit verbs (`moved`, `renamed`, `tagged`, `untagged`, `linked`, `unlinked`, `reopened`) are churn rather than outcomes and are left out. A KEY IS ABSENT RATHER THAN ZERO when nothing of that kind happened, which is why the spelling had to be published: a misspelled lookup and a genuinely quiet day are the same zero, and only one of them is true.

TaskEnvelope.title: TaskEnvelope
TaskEnvelope.description:
§4.4 — a mutation answers with the task it changed.

Named in the schema rather than returned as a bare dict so the app can drop
its tolerant envelope-or-task decoder (joy A5, 2026-08-20). The rule across
the API: a GET returns the resource, a mutation returns it wrapped, so a
mutation can gain a sibling field without changing shape.

`task` is never null: these endpoints 404 when the task does not exist
rather than answering with none. (This class was declared twice, and the
earlier copy typed `task` as optional — the later one won, so the optional
shape never reached the wire and removing it changes nothing.)

TaskOptionsComponent.title: TaskOptionsComponent
TaskOptionsComponent.description: Disambiguation. Rendered as buttons, 3 at a time (§2.7).

Todo.title: Todo
Todo.description:
One to-do. §5.

A to-do HAS tasks; it is not one (§5.1). It carries no deadline machinery of
its own — no firing, no chasing, no extensions — because if two systems
chase the same deadline the user gets buzzed twice for one thing. Setting a
reminder on a to-do means creating a task and linking it.

`due_at` IS NULLABLE AND THAT IS ORDINARY, not an edge case (§5.2). An
undated to-do cannot be overdue and cannot fail; it lives in the backlog and
the only thing the dashboard says about it is whether it has gone `stale`.

TodoEnvelope.title: TodoEnvelope
TodoEnvelope.description:
What the mutations answer with, matching `TaskEnvelope`'s shape so the
app's two domains behave the same way.

TodoEvent.title: TodoEvent
TodoEvent.description:
One thing that happened to one to-do. Append-only, never edited.

WHY THIS ROUTE EXISTS (joy, item 136): the dashboard can say a to-do has
gone stale; only the trail can say whether it was touched-and-deferred or
genuinely forgotten. Those two are identical in `updated_at`, which is the
one field a reader would otherwise reach for.

TodoEventDetail.title: TodoEventDetail
TodoEventDetail.description:
What changed, in the domain's own terms (§5, tracker item 136).

TYPED, because joy would otherwise be writing `detail["tag"]` against prose
in a board note — which is exactly what `SummaryFacts` was for its first
hour and exactly the failure item 110 was about. A misspelled key on an
untyped map is not an error, it is a blank space on a screen.

ONE COMPONENT WITH OPTIONAL FIELDS rather than ten, one per verb. joy
offered either. A discriminated union of ten shapes is more precise and
costs the client ten branches to render a list where most rows carry one
key; a single named component with every legal key typed gives the same
guarantee — no guessing at names — at a fraction of the weight. Which verb
populates which field:

  created             `title`, `dated`
  tagged / untagged   `tag`
  linked / unlinked   `task_id`
  done / cancelled /
    reopened / moved  `was` — the status it came FROM
  renamed / moved     `fields`, and `changes` on rows recorded after 0013

EVERY FIELD IS OPTIONAL AND ABSENT MEANS ABSENT. A reader must not treat a
missing `changes` as "nothing changed": the six events recorded before
2026-09-01 carry `fields` alone, because the old value was overwritten in
place and no copy was kept. That is unrecoverable, not unrecorded, and it is
the same shape as `extend_occurrence` once overwriting `scheduled_for` and
making every drift number look near zero.

TodoEvents.title: TodoEvents
TodoEvents.description: Paged, newest first, because a trail only grows.

TodoFieldChange.title: TodoFieldChange
TodoFieldChange.description:
One field, before and after.

`before` / `after` rather than `from` / `to`: `from` is a Python keyword, so
typing it would need a Pydantic alias on every read and write for no gain.
That is the same reason `SummaryFacts` carries `period_start` / `period_end`
(migration 0011), and using the same pair of words twice is worth more than
matching a phrase nobody has to type.

Both are the rendered string form, including for dates — the trail is read,
not computed against, and a client that wants to do arithmetic on a to-do's
old due date should be reading the to-do rather than its history.

TodoPriority.title: TodoPriority
TodoPriority.description:
How much a to-do wants doing, on a backlog of forty (§5, item 135).

FOUR LEVELS, NOT FIVE. Jira's five has two nobody can tell apart on a row
forty pixels tall, and a glyph that does not read at a glance is decoration.

DECLARATION ORDER IS THE SORT ORDER, here and in the Postgres enum it
mirrors, so "most important first" needs no CASE expression and no integer
column kept in step with the labels.

`Task.is_priority` IS DELIBERATELY STILL A BOOLEAN and this asymmetry is not
an oversight — see its own field. A reminder is one thing at one time and
starring it is genuinely a two-state question; a to-do sits in a backlog and
needs ordering. Different questions, different types.

UpcomingOccurrences.title: UpcomingOccurrences
UpcomingOccurrences.description:
Feeds the device alarm mirror (§2.8). Not in the parent plan's API list;
added because reminders are impossible without it.

ReminderVerb.title: ReminderVerb
ReminderVerb.description: What happened to one firing of a reminder — `tasks.occurrence_event`. Every word is distinct on purpose. `cancelled` is somebody deciding against a firing; `superseded` is its deadline moving out from under it. A reader that wants "every ending" names the ones it means: there is deliberately no coarse verb layer, because folding these two back into one word is the conflation the event stream exists to end.

SlotVerb.title: SlotVerb
SlotVerb.description: What happened to one routine slot on one logical day — `routines.slot_event`.
